summary: Defines optional extensions to the Simple Two-Way Active Measurement Protocol (STAMP) that allow measuring additional performance metrics. It also defines a STAMP Test Session Identifier, and updates RFC 8762.

plainLanguage.summary: STAMP is a way to measure delay between two points on a network by sending test packets and timing them. RFC 8972 adds optional extra fields to those packets, so a sender can ask the other end for things like its address, how its clock is set, or how a packet was classified, and can have the extra fields signed so nobody can change them.

subtitle: Optional add-on fields that let STAMP test packets carry location, timing, class-of-service and integrity data.

tldr.problem: The base Simple Two-way Active Measurement Protocol measures delay and loss with fixed-format test packets, and gives no room to ask a reflector for extra information or to protect that information.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8972 appends optional Type-Length-Value elements after the base packet: padding, location, timestamp information, class of service, direct counters, access reports, follow-up timestamps and an HMAC. It also adds a 2-octet Session Identifier to the base packet.
tldr.outcome: Senders can ask a reflector for richer measurements, while a reflector that does not understand a TLV simply flags it as unrecognized and copies it through. The document updates RFC 8762.

facts.label: Access Report retransmit
facts.value: Up to 4 times, default timer of 3 seconds

today: RFC 8972 is a Proposed Standard, published in January 2021, and it updates RFC 8762 by adding the session identifier. No RFC obsoletes it and no RFC updates it.

sections.title: Optional Extensions to STAMP
sections.content:
The Simple Two-way Active Measurement Protocol (STAMP) (RFC 8762) defines the base STAMP functionality. This document specifies the use of optional extensions that use Type-Length-Value (TLV) encoding. Such extensions enhance the STAMP base functions, such as measurement of one-way and round-trip delay, latency, packet loss, packet duplication, and out-of-order delivery of test packets. The specification defines the optional STAMP extensions, their formats, and the theory of operation. It also defines a STAMP Test Session Identifier as an update of the base STAMP specification.

In STAMP, the Session-Sender transmits test packets to the Session-Reflector. The Session-Reflector receives the packet and acts according to the configuration and the optional control information communicated in the Session-Sender's test packet. STAMP defines two different test packet formats, one for packets transmitted by the Session-Sender and one for packets transmitted by the Session-Reflector, and it supports two modes, unauthenticated and authenticated. Unauthenticated STAMP test packets are compatible on the wire with unauthenticated TWAMP-Test (RFC 5357) packets. By default, STAMP uses symmetrical packets, meaning that the size of the packet transmitted by the Session-Reflector equals the size of the packet it received.
sections.plainLanguage: STAMP is a way to measure delay between two points on a network by sending test packets and timing them. RFC 8972 adds optional extra fields to those packets, so a sender can ask the other end for things like its address, how its clock is set, or how a packet was classified, and can have the extra fields signed so nobody can change them.

sections.title: The STAMP Session Identifier
sections.content:
A STAMP Session is identified by the 4-tuple of source and destination IP addresses and source and destination UDP port numbers. A Session-Sender MAY generate a locally unique STAMP Session Identifier, the SSID. The SSID is a two-octet, non-zero unsigned integer, and the generation policy is implementation specific. An implementation MUST NOT assign the same identifier to different STAMP test sessions. If the SSID is used, it MUST be present in each test packet of the given test session, and in the unauthenticated mode it sits next to the Error Estimate field in the Session-Sender's packet and in the reflected packet.

An implementation of the Session-Reflector that supports this specification MUST identify a STAMP Session using the SSID together with elements of the usual 4-tuple. Before a test session commences, a Session-Reflector MUST be provisioned with all the elements that identify the session, and it MUST discard non-matching STAMP test packets. How that provisioning happens is outside the scope of this specification. A conforming Session-Reflector MUST copy the SSID value from the received test packet into the reflected packet.

A Session-Reflector that does not support this specification returns the zeroed SSID field in the reflected packet. The Session-Sender MAY stop the session if it receives a zeroed SSID field, and an implementation of a Session-Sender MUST support control of its behaviour in that scenario. If the session is not stopped, the Session-Sender can, for example, send a base STAMP packet or continue transmitting STAMP test packets with the SSID. The location of the SSID field in the authenticated mode is shown in the figures for the extended Session-Sender and Session-Reflector packets.
sections.plainLanguage: Two test sessions between the same pair of addresses look the same on the network. The session identifier is a small extra number that tells the reflector which session a packet belongs to. A reflector that does not know about it sends the number back as zero, and the sender can then decide whether to carry on.

sections.title: The TLV Header and Its Flags
sections.content:
The Type-Length-Value encoding scheme provides a flexible extension mechanism for optional informational elements. A TLV is an optional field in the STAMP test packet, and multiple TLVs MAY be placed in one packet. Additional TLVs may also be enclosed within a given TLV, subject to the semantics of the outer TLV. A TLV has a one-octet STAMP TLV Flags field, a one-octet Type field, and a two-octet Length field equal to the length of the Value field in octets. If a Type value falls in the Private Use range, the length MUST be at least 4 and the first four octets MUST be the vendor's Structure of Management Information Private Enterprise Code in network octet order. All multi-byte fields in the TLVs defined here are in network byte order.

The flags field carries three one-bit flags and five reserved bits. The U flag, for Unrecognized, is set by the Session-Sender to 1 before transmitting, and the Session-Reflector sets it to 1 in a TLV it did not understand, otherwise to 0. The M flag, for Malformed, is set to 0 by the Session-Sender, and the Session-Reflector sets it to 1 when it determines that the TLV is malformed, meaning the Length field is not valid for that type or the remaining length of the packet is less than the size of the TLV. The I flag, for Integrity, is set to 0 by the Session-Sender, and the Session-Reflector sets it to 1 when the STAMP extensions have failed HMAC verification. The reserved flags MUST be zeroed on transmit and ignored on receipt.

A node receiving a test packet MUST determine whether the packet is a base STAMP packet or includes one or more TLVs. It does so by comparing the value in the Length field of the UDP header with the length of the base STAMP test packet in the mode in use. If the difference is greater than the length of the UDP header, the packet includes one or more TLVs that immediately follow the base packet. A Session-Reflector that does not support STAMP extensions will not process them but will copy them into the reflected packet, while one that supports TLVs indicates the specific TLVs it did not process by setting the U flag.

A Session-Sender that receives a reflected packet with extension TLVs MUST validate each one. If the U flag is set, the system MUST skip the processing of that TLV. If the M flag is set, it MUST stop processing the remainder of the packet. If the I flag is set, it MUST discard all TLVs and stop processing the remainder of the packet.
sections.plainLanguage: Each optional field starts with a one-byte flags field, a one-byte type number, and a two-byte length. The three flags tell the sender what happened to that field: the reflector did not understand it, it was malformed, or its integrity check failed. A sender stops reading the rest of the packet when it sees the last two of those.

sections.title: Padding, Location and Timestamp TLVs
sections.content:
The Extra Padding TLV, type 1, is similar to the Packet Padding field in a TWAMP-Test packet. It SHOULD be filled with a sequence of pseudorandom numbers and MAY be filled with all zeros. Its use is RECOMMENDED to perform a STAMP test using packets larger than the base STAMP packet, and the length of the base packet is 44 octets in the unauthenticated mode or 112 octets in the authenticated mode. The Extra Padding TLV MAY be present more than once in an extended packet.

The Location TLV, type 2, lets the Session-Sender query location information from the Session-Reflector. The Session-Sender MUST NOT fill any information fields except the flags, type and length. The TLV carries the destination and source UDP port numbers of the received STAMP packet and a sequence of sub-TLVs. The sub-TLVs let the Session-Sender ask for location information with generic types, and the Session-Reflector answers with the more specific type for the address family it uses. The defined sub-TLVs are the Source MAC Address, Source EUI-48 Address, Source EUI-64 Address, Destination IP Address, Destination IPv4 Address, Destination IPv6 Address, Source IP Address, Source IPv4 Address and Source IPv6 Address. For example, if the sender asks for the Source IP Address sub-TLV, the reflector MUST answer with the Source IPv4 Address sub-TLV when the source address of the received packet is IPv4, and with the Source IPv6 Address sub-TLV otherwise.

The Location TLV MAY be used to determine the last-hop IP addresses, ports and last-hop MAC address for STAMP packets. The MAC address can indicate a path switch on the last hop, and the IP addresses and UDP ports indicate whether there is a NAT router on the path. That lets the Session-Sender identify the IP address of the Session-Reflector behind the NAT and detect changes in the NAT mapping that could result in sending STAMP packets to the wrong reflector.

The Timestamp Information TLV, type 3, lets the Session-Sender request information about how the reflector took its timestamps. It has four one-octet fields: the source of clock synchronization at the ingress of the reflector, the method by which the ingress obtained the timestamp T2, the source of clock synchronization at the egress, and the method by which the egress obtained the timestamp T3. The registered synchronization sources are NTP, PTP, SSU/BITS, the satellite systems GPS/GLONASS/LORAN-C/BDS/Galileo, and a local free-running clock. The registered timestamping methods are HW Assist, SW Local and Control Plane. The TLV may also carry optional sub-TLVs.
sections.plainLanguage: Three optional fields cover the most common extra questions. Padding makes the test packets bigger, which is useful for testing paths that handle large packets. The Location TLV asks the far end what address the packet arrived with, so a sender can spot a NAT or a change of path. The Timestamp Information TLV asks how the far end took its timestamps, so a reader knows how much of the measured delay is clock error.

sections.title: Class of Service, Counters and Access Reports
sections.content:
The Class of Service TLV, type 4, has a fixed length of 4 octets. Its DSCP1 field is the Differentiated Services Code Point the Session-Sender intends the reflector to use in the reflected packet, DSCP2 is the value received in the DSCP field at the ingress of the reflector, and the ECN field is the value received in the ECN field at that ingress. The reflector MUST copy the DSCP and ECN values from the IP header of the received packet into the DSCP2 field of the reflected packet. It then uses local policy to decide whether the class of service named by DSCP1 is permitted in its domain: if it is, the reflector sets the DSCP value in the IP header of the reflected packet to that value, and otherwise it keeps the received DSCP value and sets the RP, or Reverse Path, flag to 1. When the Session-Sender sees RP equal to 0 it can save the DSCP and ECN values for analysis of the class of service in the reverse direction; when RP is 1 only the forward direction can be analysed. Re-mapping of class of service can provide multiple services over the same network, but if it is misconfigured it is often hard to diagnose the root cause of excessive packet drops of a higher-level service. The RFC notes that using the CoS TLV in STAMP testing helps to troubleshoot that problem and to verify that DiffServ policies are processing class of service as the configuration requires.

The Direct Measurement TLV, type 5, collects the number of in-profile packets, meaning packets that form a specific data flow, that the Session-Sender and the Session-Reflector have transmitted and received. The definition of an in-profile packet is outside the scope of the document. The TLV has three four-octet counters: the Session-Sender's transmitted count, and the reflector's received and transmitted counts, each of which the reflector fills in. The reflector MUST copy the value from the sender's counter into the reflected packet before transmitting it.

The Access Report TLV, type 6, indicates changes to the access network status. Its ID field identifies the access network, with the value 1 for a 3GPP network and 2 for a non-3GPP network; a TLV with any other value MUST be discarded. Its Return Code field carries the report signal, with the registered values being Network available and Network unavailable. The reflector MUST include the TLV in the reflected packet with the same field values. The Session-Sender MUST arm a retransmission timer after sending a packet that includes this TLV, and disarm it when the reflected packet arrives. If the timer expires first, the Session-Sender MUST retransmit the packet, and this SHOULD be repeated up to four times before the procedure is aborted. The default value of the retransmission timer SHOULD be three seconds, and an implementation MUST provide control of the timer value and the number of retransmissions.
sections.plainLanguage: These three fields answer operational questions rather than timing ones. The class of service field checks that a packet is treated the way the operator intended in each direction. The counter field gives the number of matching packets each side saw. The access report field tells the far end that the user's network is up or down, and it is retransmitted a few times until the far end answers.

sections.title: The HMAC TLV
sections.content:
The STAMP authenticated mode protects the integrity of data collected in the base packet. STAMP extensions are designed to give valuable information about the condition of a network, and protecting the integrity of that data is also essential. All authenticated STAMP base packets compatible with this specification MUST additionally authenticate the optional TLVs by including the keyed Hashed Message Authentication Code TLV, with the sole exception of when there is only one TLV present and it is the Extra Padding TLV. The HMAC TLV MUST follow all the other TLVs in the packet, except the Extra Padding TLV. If it appears in any other position, the situation MUST be processed as an HMAC verification failure. The HMAC TLV MAY also be used to protect integrity in the unauthenticated mode, and an implementation of STAMP extensions MUST provide controls to enable that.

The TLV has type 8, a length of 16 octets, and a 16-octet HMAC field carrying the digest of the text of all preceding TLVs. STAMP uses HMAC-SHA-256 truncated to 128 bits (RFC 4868), and the considerations about the key that RFC 8762 lists fully apply. Key management and how the HMAC key is distributed are outside the scope of this specification. HMAC is calculated over text that is the concatenation of the Sequence Number field of the base STAMP packet and all preceding TLVs, and the digest is then truncated to 128 bits and written into the HMAC field.

If the HMAC TLV is present in the extended packet, HMAC MUST be verified before any data in the included TLVs is used. If verification by the Session-Reflector fails, the reflector MUST stop processing the received packet, MUST copy the TLVs into the reflected packet, and MUST set the I flag in each copied TLV to 1 before transmitting it. If the Session-Sender receives the reflected packet with the I flag set to 1, it MUST stop processing TLVs in that packet, and if HMAC verification by the Session-Sender fails it MUST also stop processing the TLVs in the reflected packet.
sections.plainLanguage: The HMAC TLV is a fingerprint of everything before it, computed with a key both ends share. A reflector that cannot verify the fingerprint copies the fields back with a flag saying the check failed, and the sender then ignores them. The check protects the contents from being altered, but it does not stop an old packet being replayed.

sections.title: IANA Registries
sections.content:
The document creates six subregistries. The STAMP TLV Types subregistry allocates the type numbers, where 1 to 175 need IETF Review, 176 to 239 are First Come First Served, 240 to 251 are for Experimental Use and 252 to 254 are Private Use. This document allocates 1 for Extra Padding, 2 for Location, 3 for Timestamp Information, 4 for Class of Service, 5 for Direct Measurement, 6 for Access Report, 7 for Follow-Up Telemetry and 8 for HMAC.

The STAMP TLV Flags subregistry records the three flags: bit 0 is U, Unrecognized TLV; bit 1 is M, Malformed TLV; and bit 2 is I, Integrity check failed. The STAMP Sub-TLV Types subregistry allocates the sub-TLV numbers used inside the Location TLV: 1 Source MAC Address, 2 Source EUI-48 Address, 3 Source EUI-64 Address, 4 Destination IP Address, 5 Destination IPv4 Address, 6 Destination IPv6 Address, 7 Source IP Address, 8 Source IPv4 Address and 9 Source IPv6 Address.

The STAMP Synchronization Sources subregistry lists where a clock comes from: 1 NTP, 2 PTP, 3 SSU/BITS, 4 GPS/GLONASS/LORAN-C/BDS/Galileo and 5 Local free-running. The STAMP Timestamping Methods subregistry lists how a timestamp was taken: 1 HW Assist, 2 SW Local and 3 Control Plane. The STAMP Return Codes subregistry lists the access report signals: 1 Network available and 2 Network unavailable.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC registers the numbers it uses so that other specifications can extend the same lists without collisions. The TLV type numbers 1 to 8 are the eight optional fields defined here, and the sub-TLV numbers 1 to 9 are the location questions a sender can ask.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
This document defines extensions to STAMP and inherits all the security considerations applicable to the base protocol. The HMAC TLV is defined here as well. Although the HMAC TLV protects the integrity of STAMP extensions, it does not protect against a replay attack.

To protect against a malformed TLV, an implementation of a Session-Sender and Session-Reflector MUST check the setting of the M flag and validate the Length field value.

Because the specification defines a mechanism to test DSCP mapping, it inherits all the security considerations discussed in RFC 2474. Monitoring and optional control of DSCP using the CoS TLV may be used across the Internet, so that the Session-Sender and the Session-Reflector are located in domains that use different CoS profiles. It is therefore essential that an operator verify the set of CoS values used in the Session-Reflector's domain. An implementation of a Session-Reflector SHOULD support a local policy to confirm whether the value sent by the Session-Sender can be used as the value of the DSCP field.
sections.plainLanguage: The extra fields inherit the security rules of the base protocol, with one gap: the HMAC protects the fields from being changed but does not stop a captured packet being replayed later. A reader of the results also needs to remember that the two ends may sit in networks with different class-of-service settings.

items.label: Extra Padding
items.desc: Pads the test packet; recommended when testing with packets larger than the base packet.

items.label: Location
items.desc: Asks the reflector for the addresses, ports and MAC address of the last hop.

items.label: Timestamp Information
items.desc: Asks how the reflector synchronized its clock and took its timestamps.

items.label: Class of Service
items.desc: Carries the DSCP and ECN values seen and asked for, and the reverse path flag.

items.label: Direct Measurement
items.desc: Carries the in-profile packet counters of both ends.

items.label: Access Report
items.desc: Reports whether the access network is available.

items.label: Follow-Up Telemetry
items.desc: Carries the timestamp of the previously reflected packet.

items.label: HMAC
items.desc: Carries the digest of all preceding TLVs, truncated to 128 bits.
